title: IBM plans 1,040-qubit quantum system for 2027 with new Nighthawk r3 chips
excerpt: IBM says its next quantum chip, Nighthawk r3, is designed for 520 qubits — and two linked together in 2027 would form a 1,040-qubit system.
content:
IBM says its next quantum processor is designed to run 10,000 quantum operations across 520 programmable qubits — and in 2027, the company plans to link two of the chips together into a single system with 1,040 programmable qubits.

The company announced the new chip, IBM Quantum Nighthawk r3, on Wednesday, Nov. 11, from Yorktown Heights, New York. The current-generation chip, Nighthawk r2, introduced in September, supports more than 7,500 quantum operations on 120 programmable qubits.

The r3 design carries 2,034 total physical qubits, of which 520 would be programmable, and is built to execute 10,000 quantum operations. Each r3 chip will have ten chip-to-chip connectors, called l-couplers. In a 2026 experiment, IBM linked earlier Nighthawk r1 processors with four such couplers and reported up to 99.3 percent quantum-state transfer fidelity, against a stated target of 99.9 percent.

Customers and partners including E.ON, Algorithmiq and Q-CTRL have executed more than 34 billion circuits on Nighthawk r2, IBM said, reporting performance gains of up to several times on some workloads.

The announcement is part of IBM's longer road map toward fault-tolerant quantum computing. The company targets its planned Starling system — a machine designed to run error-corrected, large-scale quantum programs — for 2029.

What the numbers do — and don't — mean

The 520- and 1,040-qubit figures are design targets, not measured performance on finished hardware. Neither the r3 chip nor the linked two-chip system is operational today, and IBM has not claimed quantum advantage — the point at which a quantum machine beats the best classical computer on a useful problem — for r3. IBM also has not given an availability date for the r3 chip itself.

The approach matters because it changes how bigger quantum machines get built. Instead of trying to cram ever more qubits onto a single chip, IBM is betting on modularity: linking smaller chips together while preserving the connections between qubits. The 2027 two-chip system will be the first real test of whether that approach holds up outside the lab.

If it works, larger quantum systems could eventually tackle problems in drug discovery, materials design and complex optimization that are out of reach for today's machines. That is a long-term prospect, not a product on shelves — and qubit counts alone do not establish fault tolerance or commercial usefulness.
